title: Body
intro: Four real things in our circle: Sean's eczema, his mom's blood pressure, his sister-in-law's acne, and what a blood test actually takes from you. Each one has treatments with solid evidence and a lot of noise around them. The goal is to know enough to ask sharp questions and spot hype.

sections.title: Eczema (Sean): what it is and the daily routine
points: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) is two problems at once: a leaky skin barrier and an immune system that overreacts.
A weak barrier lets water out and irritants in. Many people carry gene changes (like filaggrin, a skin-building protein) that make the barrier thinner.
Itch leads to scratching, which damages skin more, which itches more. Breaking that loop is the whole game.
Moisturisers (emollients) are the base treatment, not an extra. The NHS says use them at least twice a day, generously, even when skin looks clear.
Soak and seal: short lukewarm bath or shower, pat dry, then put moisturiser on within about 3 minutes so it locks the water in.
Common triggers: soap and bubble bath, sweat, heat, wool, stress, dust mites, and fragranced products. Swap soap for an emollient wash.

sections.title: Eczema (Sean): medicines that work, and diet myths
points: Steroid creams (topical corticosteroids) calm flares fast. Used in the right strength, for short bursts, they are safe. Fear of them often causes under-treatment.
Dose by fingertip unit (a line of cream from fingertip to first crease). One unit covers about two adult palms of skin.
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are steroid-free creams. They are good for the face, eyelids and folds where steroids thin the skin.
For severe eczema, a dermatologist can offer injections (biologics like dupilumab) or tablets (JAK inhibitors). These work well but are costly in SA, so check your medical aid.
Diet: the NHS says do not cut out foods unless a doctor tells you to. Food allergy matters more in babies; in adults, elimination diets rarely help and can backfire.
Real evidence: a Cochrane review found moisturisers mean fewer flares and less steroid needed. Most 'miracle' creams were no better than a plain one.

sections.title: High blood pressure (Sean's mom): the numbers and why it's silent
points: Blood pressure has two numbers. The top (systolic) is pressure when the heart squeezes. The bottom (diastolic) is pressure when it rests.
Healthy is roughly 90/60 to 120/80. High is 140/90 or more at a clinic, or 135/85 or more at home (NHS).
It is called silent because most people feel nothing. WHO says about 44% of adults with high blood pressure do not know they have it.
Over years, high pressure damages arteries, which leads to stroke, heart attack, kidney failure and dementia. Treatment cuts those risks.
South Africans eat about 6 to 11 g of salt a day. WHO's limit is under 5 g, about one teaspoon. Much of it hides in bread, stock cubes, processed meat and takeaways.
SA law has capped salt in processed foods since 2016, which helped, but home cooking and stock cubes still add a lot.

sections.title: High blood pressure: what actually lowers it
points: DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is an eating plan with lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains and low-fat dairy, and less salt and fatty meat. Trials show it lowers pressure.
Exercise helps: aim for about 150 minutes a week of brisk walking or similar.
Alcohol raises blood pressure. Cutting down helps; heavy drinking is a big driver.
Home checks need a validated upper-arm machine (one tested for accuracy; check the STRIDE BP list). Sit 5 minutes, arm at heart level, take 2 readings morning and evening for a week.
Pills matter. Most people need them for life. Stopping because you feel fine can make pressure bounce back up, because feeling fine was never the sign.

Emergency signs: very high readings (around 180/120) with chest pain, severe headache, confusion, vision loss or weakness. Face drooping or slurred speech means stroke. Call 112 from a mobile or 10177.

sections.title: Acne (sister-in-law): causes, what works, myths and scars
points: Acne starts when oil (sebum) and dead skin clog a pore, bacteria (C. acnes) grow, and the spot gets inflamed. Hormones drive the oil. It is not caused by dirty skin.

First line: benzoyl peroxide (kills bacteria, no resistance) and retinoids like adapalene (unclog pores). Start thin, every other night, and give it 8 to 12 weeks. Azelaic acid is gentler and fades dark marks.
Antibiotics should never be used alone or long-term. NICE says pair them with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid and review by about 3 months to limit resistance.
For women, the combined pill or spironolactone can help. Severe or scarring acne needs a dermatologist for isotretinoin, which works very well but needs strict pregnancy prevention and monitoring.

Diet: modest evidence that high-GI foods (sugary, white-flour foods that spike blood sugar) and milk, especially skim, worsen acne in some people. Chocolate alone has weak evidence. It's a nudge, not a cure.
Picking causes scars; early treatment prevents them. Dark marks (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation) fade over months with sunscreen. Pitted scars need dermatologist procedures.

sections.title: Drawing blood: how much, how fast it comes back, how to read it
points: An adult has about 5 litres of blood (about 8% of body weight). A test tube holds about 2 to 10 ml, so a normal panel of a few tubes is well under 1% of your blood.
A full donation is much bigger: SANBS takes 480 ml, about 10%. Even that is safe for healthy adults.
Plasma (the watery part of blood) comes back within a day or two if you drink fluids. Red cells take weeks; haemoglobin is usually back to normal in 6 to 12 weeks.
Draws matter when blood is already low: anaemia (too few red cells or low haemoglobin), babies, and long hospital stays where daily tests can add up.

FBC (full blood count) basics: haemoglobin (oxygen carrier), MCV (red cell size: small often means low iron, big can mean low B12 or folate), white cells (infection and immunity), platelets (clotting).
Reference ranges cover about 95% of healthy people, so a slightly flagged result is not automatically a problem. Trends over time and how you feel matter more.

do: Sean: keep a big tub of plain emollient (about R130 for 400 g at Dis-Chem) by the shower and moisturise straight after every wash.
Sean: at the first sign of a flare, use the prescribed steroid cream for a short burst, then step down. Don't wait it out.
Buy Sean's mom a validated upper-arm BP monitor (check the model on STRIDE BP) and log a week of morning and evening readings for her doctor.
Cut salt at home: taste before salting, use fewer stock cubes, and read bread and processed-meat labels.
For acne: start benzoyl peroxide or adapalene thin, every other night, and stick with it for 12 weeks before switching.
Ask for a copy of every blood test result and keep them in one folder so you can see trends.
ask: Which strength of steroid cream should I use, on which body parts, and for how many days?
Is my eczema bad enough for a dermatologist, or for biologic or JAK treatment, and does my medical aid cover it?
What is my mom's target blood pressure, and how should she time her pills?
Could any of her other medicines (like anti-inflammatory painkillers) be pushing her blood pressure up?
Is this acne bad enough for isotretinoin, and what monitoring would that need?
Which of my blood results are out of range, by how much, and do they need retesting?
watch_out: Myth: steroid creams always thin your skin. Short courses at the right strength are safe; under-treating eczema causes more harm.
Red flag: eczema that suddenly weeps, crusts or forms painful clustered blisters, with fever. That can be infection or eczema herpeticum and needs a doctor the same day.
Myth: 'I feel fine, so I can stop my blood pressure pills.' High pressure has no feeling. Never stop without the doctor.
Red flag: severe headache, chest pain, sudden vision change, face drooping or slurred speech. Call 112 or 10177 now.
Myth: acne comes from dirty skin, and toothpaste or lemon juice fixes spots. Both irritate and can darken marks.
Hype: 'detox' teas, eczema 'cures' and supplements sold online. If it promises to cure eczema or blood pressure, be sceptical.
Wrist and finger BP gadgets and smartwatches are often inaccurate. Use a validated upper-arm cuff.

resources.title: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
resources.source: European Society of Cardiology — European Heart Journal
resources.why: The current European rulebook on when a blood pressure reading counts as a problem, and what to aim for.
takeaways: Adds an 'elevated' band of 120–139/70–89. High blood pressure is still 140/90 or higher.
For most people on treatment, the top number should aim for 120–129, if they tolerate it.
Home readings get a bigger role in diagnosis.

resources.title: 2025 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults
resources.access: Free (open full text via the journal)
resources.why: The newest US guideline, with more on measuring blood pressure properly at home.
takeaways: General treatment target is below 130/80.
More weight on home monitoring and on checking for hidden causes.
For stage 2, start two medicines from different classes, ideally in one pill.

resources.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris
resources.source: Reynolds, Barbieri et al. — Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
resources.access: Abstract free on PubMed. Full text may need access.
resources.why: An evidence-graded ranking of what actually works for acne.
takeaways: Strongly recommends benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids and doxycycline.
Isotretinoin is strongly recommended for severe or scarring acne, or acne that fails other treatment.
Spironolactone and the combined pill get conditional recommendations.
Diet is listed as an evidence gap, not a proven cause.

resources.title: Guidelines of care for atopic dermatitis in adults: phototherapy and systemic therapies (executive summary)
resources.source: Davis, Sidbury et al. (AAD) — Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
resources.access: Abstract free on PubMed. Full text may need access.
resources.why: Ranks the newer eczema medicines, including JAK inhibitors, for adults who need more than creams.
takeaways: Strong recommendations for dupilumab, tralokinumab, abrocitinib, baricitinib and upadacitinib.
Advises against steroid pills or injections for eczema.
Most trials are short, so long-term comparisons are limited.

resources.title: Topical anti-inflammatory treatments for eczema: network meta-analysis
resources.source: Lax et al. — Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
resources.why: Compares every kind of eczema cream across 291 trials.
takeaways: 291 studies, about 46,000 people.
Potent steroid creams, JAK creams and tacrolimus 0.1% ranked among the most effective.
PDE-4 creams ranked among the least effective.
Mostly short-term trials.

resources.title: Skin: An Owner's Guide
resources.why: A readable dermatologist-written guide covering both eczema and acne.
takeaways: Published May 2026.
Covers eczema, acne and allergies.
A primer, so check specifics with a doctor.

resources.title: The Complete Guide to Family Health
resources.access: Buy, about R500 on Takealot (checked 17 Nov)
resources.why: A GP-written home reference covering blood pressure, skin and when to see a doctor.
takeaways: Plain language, all ages.
Explains how to get the most from a GP visit.
A general handbook, not a deep dive.

resources.title: Atopic eczema
resources.why: Clear basics, triggers, treatments and when to see a doctor.
takeaways: Atopic eczema causes itchy, dry skin and commonly alternates between flares and quieter periods.
Its appearance varies with skin tone, including grey, purple, lighter or darker patches.
The NHS advises applying emollients at least twice daily and continuing when skin improves.
Soap, heat, irritants, infection and other triggers can worsen symptoms, but eczema is not contagious.
Pain, warmth, pus, sudden worsening or fever need urgent assessment for infection.
The page advises against changing the diet without medical guidance and warns that emollient-contaminated fabrics catch fire more easily.

resources.title: Emollients
resources.why: Deep, practical guide to choosing and using moisturisers.
takeaways: The supplied address redirects to Eczema UK's emollient guide, following the organisation's name change from the National Eczema Society.
Emollients are unperfumed medical moisturisers rather than cosmetics with anti-ageing additives.
They leave an oily layer that helps keep water in the skin and improves barrier protection.
The guide describes more than 120 emollient products approved for NHS use, with local prescribing lists limiting choice.
A person may prefer a lighter cream or gel during the day and a greasier product at night.
Finding a product that works and is acceptable to use regularly can require trying different formulations.

resources.title: Emollients and moisturisers for eczema
resources.why: The evidence summary: moisturisers mean fewer flares; fancy ones aren't clearly better.
takeaways: The supplied short URL did not load, but the same Cochrane review was verified in its full-text archive at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6464068/.
The 2017 review included 77 studies and 6,603 participants, mainly with mild or moderate eczema.
Studies lasted an average of 6.7 weeks, limiting conclusions about long-term outcomes.
Moisturisers reduced flares and steroid use in some comparisons, but several findings rested on low-quality evidence.
Some measured severity improvements did not reach the threshold considered important to patients.
The evidence did not reliably establish one moisturiser as best, and adverse-effect reporting was limited.

resources.title: What is Eczema? Atopic Dermatitis Explained by a Dermatologist
resources.why: Short explainer on the barrier and immune sides of eczema.
takeaways: Verification limitation: the supplied YouTube ID mQ73EpeenGk did not return accessible video content.
Exact-ID searches did not establish its uploader or confirm the supplied title.
No transcript or description was available, so source-specific medical takeaways cannot be responsibly attributed to this video.
The AFSA eczema article and AAD eczema guideline in the new resources provide verified coverage while this existing entry remains unverified.

resources.title: Epi-max Cream 400g
resources.why: Cheap, plain SA emollient; about R130 (R117 on special) in Nov 2026.
takeaways: The supplied product URL did not load, but Dis-Chem's matching listing was found at https://www.dischem.co.za/epi-max-cream-400g-763.
It lists a 400 g tub containing cetomacrogol and glycerine, with paraffin ingredients in the ingredient list.
The retailer describes the cream as fragrance-free and colourant-free, and says it can be used as a soap substitute.
The listing displayed R129.99 and a promotional R116.99 when checked; these are time-sensitive retail prices.
At R129.99, the calculated price is about R32.50 per 100 g, useful for comparing pack sizes.
The page markets it for dry skin, eczema and psoriasis, but supplies no comparative clinical trial proving it is superior to other emollients.

resources.title: Heart and Stroke Foundation South Africa
resources.why: SA-specific heart health, salt advice and the Heart Mark food logo.
takeaways: The foundation's site separates heart-disease and stroke information from practical healthy-living resources.
Dedicated sections cover blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
Healthy-eating advice is paired with recipes, physical activity and smoking-cessation material.
The site describes community risk assessments, workplace wellness and a mobile clinic programme.
Heart Mark information includes product categories and an application and licensing process.
Support directories and Mended Hearts and Stroke groups offer routes beyond simply reading about risk.

resources.title: High blood pressure
resources.why: What the numbers mean, clinic vs home thresholds, and lifestyle steps.
takeaways: High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so feeling well does not exclude it.
Age, family history, excess salt, excess alcohol and other factors affect risk.
An upper-arm cuff measures pressure, and further home or ambulatory measurements may be needed after a high result.
Lifestyle changes and medicines reduce the risk of serious complications such as stroke and heart attack.
Persistent chest pain, especially with sweating or breathlessness, can signal an emergency.
The page's NHS booking advice and UK emergency numbers need local adaptation for South Africa.

resources.title: Blood pressure chart: What your reading means
resources.why: Simple chart to place any reading in a category.
takeaways: The upper number is systolic pressure and the lower number is diastolic pressure, measured in mmHg [millimetres of mercury].
The chart calls readings below 120 and below 80 normal.
It labels systolic 120 to 129 with diastolic below 80 as elevated.
It uses US stage 1 categories of systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89.
The higher category matters when the two numbers fall into different categories.
These US categories should be labelled as such beside South African or NICE guidance, because the thresholds differ.

resources.title: DASH Eating Plan
resources.source: NHLBI (US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute)
resources.why: The original DASH plan from the people who ran the trials.
takeaways: The supplied address redirects to NHLBI's current DASH eating-plan page.
DASH means Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension and provides daily and weekly food goals.
It requires no special branded foods.
The plan emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts and low-fat dairy alongside fish or poultry.
It limits saturated-fat-rich foods and sugary drinks and sweets.
The site links separate sections on following the plan, living with it and its health benefits.

resources.title: STRIDE BP validated monitor lists
resources.why: Check a BP machine is accuracy-tested before buying.
takeaways: STRIDE BP is a scientific nonprofit focused on accurate blood-pressure measurement.
Its website provides validated monitor lists rather than treating every commercially sold monitor as accurate.
At this check, the homepage reported 551 approved monitors and 294 preferred models among more than 5,000 on the market.
It identifies inaccurate devices and poor measurement technique as causes of misdiagnosis and inappropriate management.
It offers measurement training and links to research on blood-pressure measurement.
Approval and preferred-list totals change, so check the exact model against the current list when buying.

resources.title: How to measure your blood pressure at home
resources.why: Two-minute walkthrough of getting an accurate home reading.
takeaways: Verification limitation: the supplied YouTube ID wKCa9g0ob7k did not return accessible video content.
Exact-ID searches did not confirm its uploader, date or the claimed home-measurement title.
No usable transcript was found, so this research cannot attribute cuff-placement or timing instructions to that specific video.
The new British Heart Foundation hosted demonstration and NICE measurement recommendations provide verified alternatives while this entry remains unverified.

resources.title: Acne
resources.why: Plain overview of causes, pharmacy options and prescription treatments.
takeaways: Acne commonly affects the face, chest and back, and can include blackheads, whiteheads, pustules and deeper painful lumps.
It can leave scars and changes in skin colour or texture.
The NHS recommends gentle washing twice daily and products labelled non-comedogenic [designed not to clog pores].
Picking, squeezing and harsh scrubbing can worsen injury or scarring.
Medical help is appropriate for deep painful lesions, scarring, unsuccessful self-treatment or effects on mental health.

resources.title: Acne
resources.why: Deeper detail on hormones, diet evidence, isotretinoin and scars.
takeaways: DermNet defines acne as a chronic disorder of the hair follicle and oil gland involving blockage and inflammation.
Its causes include family tendency, androgen hormones, acne-associated bacteria and immune activity.
Comedones [blackheads and whiteheads], inflamed spots and deeper nodules represent different lesion types.
Most cases do not need laboratory tests; atypical features may justify skin swabs or selected hormone tests.
Treatment ranges from topical medicines to hormonal treatment, antibiotics or isotretinoin depending on severity and response.
Acne can persist beyond age 25, particularly in women.

resources.title: How to apply topical acne medication
resources.why: One-minute guide to using creams right so they work and irritate less.
takeaways: Verification limitation: the supplied YouTube ID Kh6I5eXtgSc did not return accessible video content.
Exact-ID searches did not establish a verified publisher or confirm the supplied application-demonstration title.
No transcript was available, so this entry cannot support specific advice about medication amount, application area or frequency.
The new AAD acne guideline and NICE treatment recommendations provide verified evidence while this existing video entry remains unverified.

resources.title: The Skincare Bible
resources.why: No-nonsense skin book with a strong acne section and myth-busting.
takeaways: The supplied publisher path did not load, but the matching ISBN was found at https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/305603/the-skincare-bible-by-mahto-dr-anjali/9780241309100.
Penguin identifies the author as consultant dermatologist Dr Anjali Mahto and dates this edition to 5 April 2018.
The publisher describes coverage of acne, rosacea, pigmentation and morning and evening routines.
Its description rejects homemade face masks as a cure for acne and lilac water as a way to reduce scarring.
The book also discusses stress, pollution, diet and changes in skin with age.
These points are based on the publisher's synopsis rather than a full-text reading, so specific treatment claims need checking against current guidelines.

resources.title: How your body replaces blood
resources.why: How plasma, red cells and iron recover after blood is taken.
takeaways: The page discusses blood donation, describing an average adult blood volume of about 10 pints and a donation of about one pint.
Kidney cells detect reduced oxygen delivery and release erythropoietin, which signals bone marrow to make more red cells.
The body makes about two million red blood cells each second.
The service says haemoglobin usually returns to normal six to 12 weeks after a donation.
Iron stores help replace lost haemoglobin, while drinking fluids helps replace the water component of blood.
The page's 12-week male and 16-week female donation intervals are NHS Blood and Transplant rules, not South African rules or recovery times for routine small blood samples.

resources.title: Blood tests
resources.why: What happens during a blood test and the common types.
takeaways: Blood tests can investigate symptoms, assess risk and monitor a condition or treatment.
The page distinguishes a full blood count, glucose, kidney-related tests, a lipid profile and thyroid-related testing.
Preparation depends on the test, so follow specific instructions about fasting or medicines rather than changing medicines independently.
A sample is usually taken from a vein near the elbow with a needle and collected in a tube for laboratory testing.
Temporary bruising or swelling can occur, and telling the collector about needle anxiety can help.
Results need an explanation and a follow-up plan; contact the requesting service if expected results do not arrive.

resources.title: Full blood count: what it tells your doctor about your health
resources.why: Short, plain explainer of the most common blood test.
takeaways: Verification limitation: the supplied YouTube ID HJO2ZmGtYHc did not return accessible video content.
Exact-ID searches did not confirm who made it or establish that it covers the claimed full-blood-count topic.
No transcript or description was available, so claims about blood-cell counts or diagnostic meanings cannot be attributed to this video.
The existing NHS blood-test page and new MedlinePlus results guide provide verified explanations while this video entry remains unverified.

resources.title: Atopic Eczema
resources.why: A detailed South African explanation of the skin barrier, allergy testing and treatment.
takeaways: Skin-barrier damage lets water escape and irritants enter, which can drive further inflammation.
Filaggrin is a skin-barrier protein whose inherited abnormalities can contribute to eczema.
More than half of children with eczema who have raised food-allergy antibodies may not actually be allergic to those foods.
The page distinguishes treating a flare from intermittent maintenance treatment on areas that repeatedly flare.
It offers downloadable action plans, wet-wrap guidance and a list of moisturisers marketed for eczema in South Africa.

resources.title: Atopic dermatitis clinical guideline
resources.why: Shows how treatment escalates when basic skin care is insufficient.
takeaways: Strong topical-treatment recommendations include moisturisers, corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors [non-steroid anti-inflammatory medicines].
Bathing and wet wraps receive conditional recommendations, reflecting less certain evidence or context-dependent choices.
Systemic options [treatments acting throughout the body] include targeted biologic medicines and JAK inhibitors [medicines affecting immune signals].
The guideline recommends against systemic corticosteroids for routine atopic dermatitis management.
The 2025 focused update adds recommendations for newer treatments, including lebrikizumab and nemolizumab with topical therapy.
These are US clinical recommendations, so South African registration, access and scheme cover need separate checks.

resources.title: What is the best way to use topical corticosteroids to treat people with eczema?
resources.why: Tests common steroid-use rules rather than treating every routine as established fact.
takeaways: Moderate and potent steroids probably control moderate or severe eczema better than mild steroids.
Potent steroids applied once daily probably work as well as twice-daily or more frequent use for flares.
Using steroid treatment on two days each week probably reduces relapse compared with reactive treatment alone.
Reported skin thinning was uncommon, but adverse effects were poorly reported and studies were often short.
The review found no trials comparing branded with generic topical steroids or establishing the best gap between steroid and emollient application.

resources.title: Topical corticosteroids and withdrawal reactions
resources.source: UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
resources.why: A regulator's balanced account of steroid benefits, overuse and withdrawal concerns.
takeaways: Skin conditions can return after treatment stops, and this does not automatically identify a withdrawal syndrome.
Severe topical steroid withdrawal reactions are thought to be rare, but their frequency is unknown.
Reported reactions usually follow frequent or prolonged use of strong steroids, for example longer than 6 to 12 months in adults.
Sensitive sites such as the face and genitals are more commonly involved in reported reactions.
Symptoms returning within days or weeks warrant medical advice before re-treating the area.

resources.title: Acne clinical guideline
resources.why: Separates established acne medicines from heavily advertised options with weaker support.
takeaways: Recommended topical options include benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, azelaic acid and selected antibiotics.
The guideline favours combining topical treatments with different mechanisms of action.
Systemic antibiotic use should be limited and accompanied by benzoyl peroxide and other topical treatment.
Options for selected patients include combined oral contraceptives and spironolactone.
Oral isotretinoin is among the recommended systemic treatments, with selection depending on disease severity and treatment history.

resources.title: Acne vulgaris: management, recommendations
resources.why: Gives a clear treatment timetable and addresses pregnancy, antibiotics and referral.
takeaways: Initial treatment is normally offered as a 12-week course, selected with the patient.
One first-line option is a fixed combination of adapalene and benzoyl peroxide, provided it is suitable for the person.
At review, an oral antibiotic can stop if acne has cleared while topical treatment continues.
Antibiotic-containing treatment beyond six months should be exceptional and reviewed every three months.
Topical retinoids and oral tetracyclines are contraindicated during pregnancy and when planning pregnancy.
Scarring, psychological impact and inadequate response influence referral; the original guideline has subsequent amendments.

resources.title: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, recommendations
resources.why: Explains confirmation, home averages and individual targets for older adults.
takeaways: Home confirmation uses two seated measurements at least one minute apart, morning and evening, for at least four days and ideally seven.
Discard day-one readings and average the remaining measurements.
Confirmation normally combines a clinic reading of at least 140/90 with a home or daytime average of at least 135/85 mmHg.
For people aged 80 or over, its usual home treatment target is below 145/85, with judgement for frailty and multiple illnesses.
A standing fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic warrants assessment; treatment targets may need to use standing pressure.
The guideline was first published in 2019 and includes later amendments, including 2026 healthy-living advice.

resources.title: Monitoring people's blood pressure in their homes leads to better control, study finds
resources.why: South African reporting showing that care delivery can matter as much as drug choice.
takeaways: The reported KwaZulu-Natal study assigned 774 adults to clinic care or one of two home-care models.
Home care combined blood-pressure monitoring, nurse review and medicine delivery by community health workers.
At six months, blood pressure was controlled in 32.5% of the clinic group, 57.4% of the home-care group and 61.3% of the enhanced home-care group.
Compared with clinic care, systolic pressure was lower by 7.9 mmHg and 9.1 mmHg in the two home-care groups.
The article identifies travel costs, queues, equipment problems and overloaded nurses as barriers to clinic-based care.
At publication, costs and performance in urban settings still needed investigation, so the study does not establish an available Edenvale service.

resources.title: Reducing sodium intake to reduce blood pressure and risk of cardiovascular diseases in adults
resources.why: A concise evidence-based target for interpreting salt and sodium labels.
takeaways: WHO recommends adults reduce sodium intake to less than 2 g per day.
That amount corresponds to about 5 g of salt rather than 2 g of salt.
The purpose is to reduce blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.
Population interventions should reduce sodium while increasing potassium through foods.
The resource links recommendations to supporting reviews rather than treating individual willpower as the only intervention.

resources.title: Use of lower-sodium salt substitutes: WHO guideline
resources.why: Explains why potassium-based salt substitutes are useful for some people and unsuitable for others.
takeaways: WHO conditionally suggests potassium-containing lower-sodium substitutes if adults choose to use table salt.
The recommendation sits alongside the stronger recommendation to reduce total sodium intake.
It excludes people with kidney impairment or other conditions that compromise potassium excretion.
It is intended for adults and does not extend to pregnant women or children.
The guideline is an 82-page evidence-informed document published on 27 January 2025.

resources.title: Mayo Clinic Q and A: What to expect during a blood draw
resources.source: Fiona Craig; Mayo Clinic News Network
resources.why: Puts a routine sample in proportion and explains the procedure without mystery.
takeaways: Ask which tests are being collected and why, including whether fasting is needed.
Hydration and warmth can help preparation, subject to the testing instructions.
Checking full name and date of birth helps keep the sample attached to the correct medical record.
The article describes an adult blood volume of approximately 5,000 mL, much larger than an ordinary sample.
It says dizziness around a routine draw is usually related to anxiety rather than the amount collected.
Hand veins can bruise more readily than accessible veins near the elbow.

resources.title: How to understand your lab results
resources.source: MedlinePlus; US National Library of Medicine
resources.why: A bookmark for interpreting reference intervals, units and uncertainty.
takeaways: A reference range is based on results from groups of healthy people and can differ by population.
Healthy people can have a result outside the reference range.
A result within the range does not guarantee that no health problem exists.
Laboratories can use different methods and ranges, so the range on the actual report matters.
Using the same laboratory can help when following changes over time.
Units are part of the result, so numbers should not be compared without checking how they were measured.

resources.title: Prescribed Minimum Benefits
resources.why: The regulator's starting point for checking the older parent's hypertension entitlement.
takeaways: PMBs establish minimum benefits regardless of the medical-scheme option selected.
Hypertension appears among the 26 Chronic Disease List conditions.
Cover for a listed chronic condition includes related consultations and tests as well as medication.
Schemes can use formularies, designated providers and treatment protocols to manage the benefit.
The published treatment algorithms establish minimum standards below which scheme treatment should not fall.
Clinical records help support an alternative when a formulary medicine is ineffective or causes adverse effects.

resources.title: Pharmaceutical Economic Evaluation and medicine-pricing databases
resources.source: South African National Department of Health
resources.why: The official source for checking declared medicine prices and pricing notices.
takeaways: The site publishes downloadable private-sector medicine-price databases.
The data include single exit prices, ex-manufacturer prices and logistics-fee fields.
Discontinued medicines remain listed, so a database entry does not prove current availability.
Separate sections contain dispensing-fee notices and single exit price adjustment documents.
Use a dated database and the applicable final notice when checking a pharmacy bill, because prices and fees change.

resources.title: Medicine Price Registry
resources.why: An accessible consumer tool for finding medicine prices and possible generic alternatives.
takeaways: Search results can help identify possible generic alternatives to a branded medicine.
The tool explains that a dispensing fee may be added to the single exit price.
Its displayed consumer totals include VAT, while the fee explanation identifies amounts excluding VAT.
The site warns that allowed fees may change and its information may not be fully current.
At this research check, it displayed medicine data collected on 26 May 2026, so compare current quotes with the official database.

resources.title: Quality and Bioequivalence guideline
resources.source: South African Health Products Regulatory Authority
resources.why: The local regulator's technical reference behind claims about medicine quality and equivalence.
takeaways: The guideline addresses new registration applications and variations to registered products.
It states SAHPRA's current expectations for safety, efficacy and quality.
Alternative technical approaches need scientific justification rather than marketing assurances.
SAHPRA can request additional information when needed to assess a medicine.
The landing page identifies version 9 dated 23 October 2025 and separates the current download from archived versions.

resources.title: Southern African Hypertension Society guidelines
resources.why: A local professional reference for understanding why imported blood-pressure charts differ.
takeaways: The page links South African hypertension guidelines and international guidance.
It includes the society's 2019 commentary on American hypertension guidelines.
It provides a 2015 medical-practitioner management algorithm and a 2016 nursing algorithm.
The 2015 algorithm lists targets below 140/90, or below 150/90 for people older than 80.
The society states that individual medicine and device choices require a medical consultation; the linked documents' dates should be checked.

resources.title: Find an accredited DSSA dermatologist
resources.why: A professional-directory starting point when looking for a skin specialist near Edenvale.
takeaways: The page is a directory for finding accredited Dermatology Society of South Africa dermatologists.
It offers a location-oriented search for skin specialists.
It is a route to locating a clinician rather than an eczema or acne treatment guideline.
The directory does not itself establish a medical-scheme network agreement.
Its listing is not a quotation or a guarantee of appointment availability, so those details need confirmation with the practice.

resources.title: How medicines pricing works in SA and how it might change in future
resources.source: Dr Andy Gray; Spotlight, Inside The Box
resources.why: An expert explainer of price regulation, supply-chain income and transparency gaps.
takeaways: Public tenders and private single exit prices operate as separate purchasing systems.
The National Drug Policy dates to 1996, while the pricing reforms took effect after legislation and court challenges in the following decade.
Private final sellers can add a regulated dispensing fee, while wholesalers receive a logistics fee within the supply chain.
The column argues that initial launch prices remain a weakness even when later increases are limited.
Pharmacy chains owning wholesalers can receive logistics income that patients do not directly see on a dispensing bill.
Gray questions opaque commercial incentives without quantifying them; his February 2026 fee and adjustment examples are dated, not current quotations.

resources.title: Clean: The New Science of Skin
resources.source: James Hamblin; Riverhead Books / Penguin Random House
resources.why: Adds the history and commercial culture of hygiene to the clinical reading.
takeaways: The publisher's description frames skin care as both a scientific topic and a cultural practice.
Hamblin interviews dermatologists, microbiologists, allergy specialists and people selling skin products.
The book examines the skin microbiome [microbes living on the skin] and emerging probiotic claims.
It questions whether everyday standards of cleanliness reliably correspond to better health.
The publisher describes his personal experiment with giving up showers; this is a narrative experiment rather than a clinical trial.
These points are verified from the publisher's description, not a full-text reading; use the book for context rather than a treatment protocol.

resources.title: Check your blood pressure: Know Your Numbers
resources.why: An official page hosting a nurse demonstration, with a guide and diary beside it.
takeaways: The hosted demonstration covers fastening the monitor cuff, choosing when to measure and reading the display.
The accompanying page stresses that high blood pressure often has no obvious symptoms.
Its measurement advice highlights feeling calm and sitting upright for a reliable reading.
A linked diary supports recording readings rather than relying on memory.
The page also promotes BHF's monitor shop, so use independent validation lists when choosing a device.
These takeaways reflect the accessible host-page text; a separate video transcript was not available in this research.

who_pays: South African households pay through taxes, medical-scheme contributions and direct payments for consultations, medicines and laboratory tests.
Public clinics use state-funded services and medicines bought through public tenders; these prices differ from private pharmacy prices.
Hypertension is one of the 26 conditions on the Chronic Disease List [CDL], so qualifying diagnosis, treatment and care fall within prescribed minimum benefits [PMBs] on every medical-scheme option.
Schemes can require registration, a formulary [covered medicine list] and designated service providers [DSPs]; choosing another brand or provider can create a co-payment.
Eczema and acne are not themselves CDL conditions, so routine cover depends on the option and circumstances rather than an automatic chronic entitlement.
who_decides: SAHPRA assesses medicine safety, quality and effectiveness; registration does not itself decide the medicine's price or whether a scheme pays.
The Health Minister and Pricing Committee regulate private-sector medicine pricing and permitted price adjustments, while public procurement uses tenders.
Clinicians and patients choose treatment using the diagnosis, severity, other conditions, pregnancy plans and the person's priorities.
Medical schemes set formularies and provider networks within legal PMB requirements, and the Council for Medical Schemes oversees compliance.
The Department of Health also sets sodium limits for specified processed foods, so food manufacturers help determine salt exposure before anyone reaches for a salt shaker.
who_profits: Manufacturers earn revenue from branded and generic medicines; patents and the number of competing suppliers can affect their bargaining power.
Pharmacies earn dispensing fees, while distributors receive logistics fees within the medicine supply chain.
Andy Gray's Spotlight analysis identifies an extra revenue route when a pharmacy chain owns its wholesaler, and describes limits to public visibility of commercial arrangements.
Private clinicians, laboratories, device sellers and skincare companies receive payment for their services or products; a commercial interest does not by itself prove a treatment is ineffective.
Medical schemes pool members' money, while administrators and managed-care businesses charge for running services; evaluating their incentives requires separating these organisations.
what_it_means_for_us: Ask the older parent's scheme for written hypertension registration, its covered medicines, approved pharmacy and consultation and testing rules.
Request the medicine's active ingredient, strength, pack size, single exit price [SEP] and dispensing fee so a cheaper generic comparison is meaningful.
Use a validated upper-arm monitor with the correct cuff and a clinician-agreed recording plan before interpreting isolated readings.
For skin care, judge a simple treatment plan over the agreed weeks using symptoms, photographs and side effects rather than buying a succession of advertised products.
For each blood test, ask what question it answers, what result would change care and how results will be explained; pregnancy plans should be discussed before acne medicines are chosen.

deep_sections.title: Eczema: a leaky barrier and an immune loop
points: Eczema involves both impaired skin protection and inflammation [an immune response that causes swelling and irritation].
Filaggrin [a protein involved in the skin barrier] helps explain why inherited differences can make skin lose water more easily.
Water loss, irritant entry and scratching can reinforce each other, so treating itch alone may leave the loop running.
Emollients [medical moisturisers] support the barrier, while topical corticosteroids [anti-inflammatory skin medicines] treat inflammation.
The 2017 Cochrane moisturiser review supports fewer flares but does not establish one universally best brand.
Cochrane's 2022 steroid review found that once-daily potent steroid treatment probably works as well as more frequent application for flares.
A clinician may prescribe intermittent treatment on recurring sites after a flare settles; this is called proactive maintenance.
Steroid strength, body site and duration matter more than a blanket claim that all steroids are dangerous or harmless.
The UK medicines regulator recognises severe withdrawal reactions, thought to be rare, but says their true frequency is unknown.
A positive allergy test can show sensitisation [immune recognition] without proving that eating the food causes symptoms.
AFSA advises expert assessment before food exclusions, especially because restrictive diets can create nutritional harm.
Painful blisters, rapidly worsening eczema, fever or feeling ill need prompt medical assessment for infection, including eczema herpeticum [a herpes infection of eczema skin].
Inflammation can look purple, grey or darker brown on darker skin, so redness alone is a poor measure of severity.

Persistent disease despite a well-used plan can justify reassessing the diagnosis or discussing specialist treatments; US guideline recommendations do not establish South African availability or funding.

deep_sections.title: An older parent's blood pressure: measurement before targets
points: Systolic pressure [the upper number] reflects pressure when the heart contracts, while diastolic pressure [the lower number] reflects pressure between beats.
Age-related artery stiffness can raise the upper number even when the lower number is not high.
A stressful clinic visit can raise pressure temporarily; white-coat hypertension means clinic readings are high while out-of-clinic readings are lower.
Masked hypertension is the opposite pattern, with apparently normal clinic readings but high readings elsewhere.
A validated device, correct cuff and consistent seated technique help prevent measurement error from becoming a diagnosis.
US categories in Mayo's chart start stage 1 hypertension at 130/80, while NICE confirmation uses clinic readings of at least 140/90 and a home or daytime average of at least 135/85.
A diagnosis threshold and a treatment target answer different questions, so ask which local guideline and measurement setting the clinician is using.
The SA Hypertension Society's published 2015 algorithm uses a target below 140/90, or below 150/90 above age 80; its date matters when comparing newer guidance.
NICE recommends checking standing pressure in people aged 80 or over and in those with relevant symptoms, because treatment can worsen postural hypotension [a pressure drop on standing].
An older person's target should account for frailty, falls, kidney function and treatment tolerance rather than age alone.
The SPRINT subgroup aged 75 or over benefited from intensive treatment, but it excluded important groups such as people with diabetes, prior stroke or nursing-home residence.
Diuretics [medicines that increase salt and water excretion], calcium-channel blockers and medicines acting on blood-pressure hormones lower pressure through different routes.
Kidney function and blood salts may need monitoring when medicines are started or changed; a normal reading on treatment is not a reason to stop it independently.
Very high repeated readings need prompt clinical advice; chest pain, new weakness, confusion or severe breathlessness require emergency assessment rather than waiting for a home diary.

deep_sections.title: Acne: blocked follicles, hormones and slow evidence
points: Acne develops in the hair-follicle and oil-gland unit through blockage, oil production, bacteria and inflammation.
A comedone [blocked follicle] can form a blackhead or whitehead; a blackhead is not evidence of dirty skin.
Scrubbing or repeatedly changing strong products can add irritation without fixing the processes that cause acne.
Retinoids [vitamin A-related medicines] help prevent blocked follicles, while benzoyl peroxide reduces acne-associated bacteria without being an antibiotic.
Combining treatments can target different processes, but several irritating products started together can make the plan hard to tolerate.
NICE uses a 12-week first treatment course, because visible improvement commonly takes several weeks.
Antibiotics should have a review and stopping plan; AAD recommends benzoyl peroxide alongside antibiotic treatment to limit resistance [bacteria becoming less responsive].
Hormonal treatments can help selected women even when acne is not evidence of a dangerous hormone disorder.
Acne with irregular periods or other signs of excess androgen activity [effects of hormones such as testosterone] can justify targeted assessment rather than a routine hormone panel for everyone.
In the SAFA trial, spironolactone's advantage was clearer at 24 weeks than 12 weeks, showing why an early comparison can miss later benefit.
Spironolactone affects blood pressure and potassium as well as hormone signalling, so suitability and monitoring depend on the person's health and other medicines.
Pregnancy plans change acne treatment choices: NICE advises against topical retinoids and oral tetracyclines during pregnancy or while planning it.
Oral isotretinoin can cause serious fetal harm and requires a carefully supervised pregnancy-prevention and monitoring plan when relevant.
NICE finds insufficient evidence to prescribe a particular acne diet; claims that one food explains every breakout overstate the evidence.
Scarring, persistent dark marks and psychological distress are valid reasons to seek treatment before acne becomes severe.

deep_sections.title: Blood draws: volume, fainting and what results mean
points: An ordinary diagnostic blood draw removes a small sample from a vein, while a whole-blood donation removes hundreds of millilitres.
Mayo describes an adult blood volume of roughly 5,000 mL; as an illustration, a 20 mL collection would be about 0.4% of that volume.
The actual volume depends on the requested tests and tubes, so the person taking the sample can explain the planned amount.
Fainting around needles can be vasovagal [an automatic nervous-system response that lowers blood pressure and sometimes heart rate], rather than evidence of major blood loss.
Tell the collector about previous fainting and ask to lie down if needed.
A bruise usually means a little blood leaked into surrounding tissue; applying pressure after needle removal helps limit it.
The kidneys release erythropoietin [a signal for red-cell production], and bone marrow makes replacement red cells using nutrients including iron.
NHS Blood and Transplant's weeks-long haemoglobin recovery figures describe donation and should not be applied unchanged to a small routine sample.
Repeated ICU sampling can contribute to iatrogenic anaemia [low haemoglobin partly caused by medical care], especially in people already seriously ill.
STRATUS tested smaller tubes in intensive care; its primary analysis did not show a statistically clear reduction in transfusion, although a larger secondary analysis did.
A full blood count measures blood cells but does not directly measure every nutrient or exclude every cause of tiredness.
A reference range [the laboratory's comparison interval] is not a boundary between perfect health and disease.
Use the units and reference interval on the actual report, and interpret trends alongside symptoms and medicines.
Fasting is test-specific, and medicine changes should follow the requesting clinician's instructions rather than a blanket rule.
Learning about blood tests cannot establish why the pregnancy loss happened; a cause would require the relevant records and clinical investigation.

deep_sections.title: The price of care and the salt already in food
points: SEP [single exit price] is South Africa's regulated private medicine supply price, not a promise that every pharmacy bill will be identical.
A dispensing fee can be added, and medical-scheme reimbursement can differ from the retail amount.
Public-sector tender prices use state purchasing power and must not be confused with private SEPs.
A regulated annual increase does not prove the starting price is good value; Andy Gray's analysis identifies the initial launch price as a weakness in the framework.
Generic comparisons must match the active ingredient, strength and dosage form; two medicines for the same condition are not automatically interchangeable.
SAHPRA's bioequivalence framework [assessment of comparable medicine availability in the body] is part of how generic quality and interchangeability are assessed.
A brand name, expensive packaging or a long ingredient list is not evidence of better clinical results.
For PMBs, distinguish a preference for another brand from a documented medical reason that the formulary option fails or causes harm.
Ask for a written funding decision and keep clinical evidence for a formulary exception or scheme complaint.
South Africa's sodium rules were introduced in stages in 2016 and 2019 across 13 processed-food categories, making reformulation a population-level prevention measure.
The 2025 rural cohort study found estimated sodium excretion fell by about 0.23 g per day from the first to third survey wave; an observational study cannot isolate the law from every other change.
Sodium and salt use different numbers: 2,000 mg sodium equals about 5 g salt, including salt already present in food.
Bread, processed meats, sauces and stock products can contribute salt even when a meal does not taste especially salty.
WHO's potassium-containing salt-substitute advice excludes people with impaired potassium excretion and does not apply to pregnant women or children.
For an older parent with kidney disease or potassium-raising medicines, check with the clinician before replacing table salt with a potassium product.
Read evidence quality and funding disclosures together; a commercial tie deserves scrutiny but does not substitute for assessing the study's methods and results.
